Cubital tunnel syndrome

In 64 patients, PBM improved selected cubital-tunnel outcomes more than sham in the short term. At three months, most outcomes were similar, although the PRUNES-Pain subscale still favored PBM. In a separate randomized comparison, manual therapy improved several nerve and sensory measures more than combined PBM and ultrasound.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

In 64 patients, PBM improved selected cubital-tunnel outcomes more than sham in the short term. At three months, most outcomes were similar, although the PRUNES-Pain subscale still favored PBM. In a separate randomized comparison, manual therapy improved several nerve and sensory measures more than combined PBM and ultrasound.

Summary of the Evidence

Two randomized clinical publications directly address cubital tunnel syndrome. One is a sham-controlled trial of PBM added to a splint and exercise program. The other compares a PBM-plus-ultrasound treatment package with manual therapy. No animal, in-vitro or review publication was identified in the exact category, and the two trials appear to represent separate clinical cohorts.

Human and clinical evidence

Yağcı et al. randomized 64 people with cubital tunnel syndrome to PBM or sham alongside conservative care. Active treatment favored selected short-term outcomes. At three months, most outcomes were similar, although the PRUNES-Pain subscale still favored PBM (Yağcı et al. 2024). A 2025 randomized comparison tested manual therapy against PBM combined with ultrasound. Both groups improved after treatment, while manual therapy produced greater improvement on several nerve-conduction, ultrasound and sensory measures (Wieczorek and Wolny 2025). Because PBM was paired with ultrasound in that study, its independent contribution cannot be determined.

Animal evidence

No relevant animal study was identified in the mapped category.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No standalone in-vitro or ex-vivo study was identified.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The sham-controlled trial used a 685-nm red laser pulsed at 10 Hz, with 15 sessions over three weeks. The other study used a combined 658- and 808-nm device with ultrasound settings alongside the manual-therapy comparison. These are different treatment packages and should not be pooled as tests of one PBM protocol. The first trial also evaluated PBM within usual conservative care, not as a replacement for it.

Interpretation

The evidence supports a possible short-term improvement in selected symptoms and nerve measures, with no demonstrated advantage at three months in the sham-controlled trial. The active-comparator study does not identify whether PBM itself contributed to its results. Independent sham-controlled trials with clearly reported doses and sustained functional outcomes would clarify the size and durability of any effect.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow for short-term pain and nerve-related outcomes Very low for sustained benefit or PBM without ultrasound co-treatment
Publications and records2 unique titles

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

The 64-person sham-controlled trial supports a short-term effect. By three months, most outcomes were similar, although the PRUNES-Pain subscale still favored PBM. A second randomized study compared a PBM-plus-ultrasound package with manual therapy, so it cannot isolate PBM. Larger trials should use sham control, standard nerve outcomes and follow-up beyond treatment.
